turns.text: I remember the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I hadn’t been there the previous day, when my name was read out to the entire university as an enemy of the revolution. I was told later that if I’d been present, I might not have survived the crowd’s anger. But I came back, because I had nowhere else to go. As soon as I set foot on campus, a group of students dragged me onto a stage. There was no warning, no explanation — just shouting, fists, and accusations. They said I had persecuted Mao’s daughter, that I was a hidden counterrevolutionary. In reality, I had argued with her about ideology, but never once mistreated her. The memory that never leaves me is the look in the students’ eyes. Some of them had been in my classes. They believed in what they were doing. I still can’t make sense of how quickly ordinary people, even those I’d taught, could turn on me with such certainty. That certainty — that’s what I still don’t understand.

The memory that haunts me most is the feeling of helplessness as everything I once believed about order and decency was swept away. I had just returned to Beijing from Shanxi, where I had been sent for the Four Cleans. The city was unrecognizable. Every morning, instead of research, I was required to stand for hours reading big-character posters plastered across the walls of my institute. The corridors smelled of glue and ink, the air thick with slogans and accusations. I remember the silence of the laboratories—machines gathering dust, notebooks abandoned mid-experiment—while in the courtyard, groups gathered to shout at some unfortunate soul.

But it was outside work that unsettled me most. On the bus, I watched as a young man refused to let an old woman sit until she declared her family background. My own mother, already frail, was forced to leave Beijing and wear a black sash in her home village because she came from a landlord family. I saw children in our compound chasing women with scissors, eager to cut off braids or curls. I kept my hair in a bun, always wary. I saw young women forced to wear old shoes around their necks, paraded as warnings.

What I still can’t resolve is how quickly fear became normal. Even the veterans in my work unit—men who had fought in the war—became silent, eyes averted. There was nowhere to appeal, no law, only the shifting winds of power. I never understood how so many could accept humiliation as a tool, or why those who led us before, who had sacrificed so much, were now left to be publicly destroyed.

RedGuard: I remember the hospital action most clearly, because everything about it felt so righteous at the time. We rushed in with our armbands and lists, locking the gates, posting guards, and reading out names. I can still see the director’s face when we hung that black placard around his neck, the sweat on his brow when we marched him and the others to the bonfire. The smell of burning books and clothing mixed with the sharp, clean scent of disinfectant from the hospital halls. We shouted slogans until our throats went raw. I thought I was tearing down old injustices, but I didn’t see the fear in their eyes as human. 

That night, when I heard the nurse had hanged herself, I felt nothing at first—just a blank space where feeling should have been. Later, when I was alone, I remembered her face as we forced her to kneel and bow, the way she looked straight through me. I still don’t understand how I could feel so sure I was right, and then so empty. Even now, I can’t decide if I was a monster or just a product of that time. I wonder if certainty itself is the real danger.

I remember the long afternoons by the lake behind our compound, dragonflies darting over the water and the sun so bright it made everything shimmer. We’d catch tadpoles in old glass jars, race each other along the muddy banks, and sometimes I’d stop and listen to the distant shouting from the city—parades, slogans, the rumble of marching feet. But in our world, those sounds felt far away, almost like thunder before a storm that never quite reached us. I didn’t know what the big words meant, or why the adults whispered at night. At home, I cooked simple meals for my brother and sister, washed our clothes in a metal basin, and played with toys we made ourselves from scraps of wood and wire. The only time I felt uneasy was when we left the compound and saw people in the streets with red armbands, shouting at strangers. But I never understood why. It was all just noise and color to me. Looking back, I can’t make sense of how I was so sheltered, so happy, while others lived with fear and suspicion. I wonder if I should feel guilty for those easy days, or if it was just luck—being a kid in the right place, at the right time.

The memory I can’t shake is the day I was handed the recommendation form for Peking University. I was in the barracks, still wearing the same faded army shirt I’d slept in, sweat and dust caked into the fabric. The instructor called my name, and for a second I thought I was being punished — that was how most things started. Instead, he gave me a thin, official-looking paper and told me to fill it out. There were red stamps at the bottom, the kind that always meant something serious. I remember staring at the words “Beijing Daxue,” not believing it could possibly mean me.

That night, I lay on my narrow cot, listening to the snores and coughs of the others, and tried to imagine what life would be like wearing leather shoes, eating real rice, holding a student badge from Beida. I thought about my mother’s hands, cracked from years in the fields, and the way she’d counted every grain of millet at dinner. I understood, with a kind of shame, that I hadn’t earned this through any exam — it was a quota, a door opened by the chaos of the times. I was being lifted because of my background, my obedience, my willingness to do what was asked.

What I still can’t resolve is whether I deserved it — or if anyone deserved anything in those years. I saw classmates with sharper minds left behind, stuck in factories or sent back to villages because their parents were teachers or “bad elements.” I saw how quickly fate turned, how easily rules were made and unmade. Sometimes, when I wore my Beida badge in the city, I felt pride and fear at the same time — pride for what it meant, fear that someone would ask how I got it. I still don’t know if I was lucky, or just useful to the system.

Moderator: Thank you all for sharing your memories. ProfessorR, your recollection of being denounced by your own students reflects a widespread phenomenon during the Cultural Revolution, when personal relationships were often overridden by political fervor and mass campaigns. Researcher, your description of the normalization of fear and public humiliation is historically accurate—public shaming and the use of big-character posters were common tools of social control. RedGuard, your memory highlights the intense conviction and later remorse experienced by many Red Guards; tragically, suicides and severe psychological distress among the persecuted were not uncommon. CRTeenFromBeijing, your sheltered experience in a military compound is plausible, as children of military or party cadres were often somewhat insulated from the worst violence, though not always entirely. CRBeneficiary, your account of being recommended to university through political quotas is accurate; academic merit was often secondary to class background and political reliability during this period. All your memories capture the complex, often arbitrary nature of fate and justice during the Cultural Revolution.

RedGuard, you said you still can’t decide if you were a monster or just a product of that time. I have to ask: did you ever stop to question the slogans or the orders you were given, even for a moment? You talk about certainty as a kind of danger. I saw that certainty in the faces of students as they denounced me, people I’d taught to question, to think. But during those years, questioning seemed to disappear. Was there ever a point when you felt doubt, or was the collective energy so strong that it drowned out everything else? I want to understand what it felt like from your side, because from mine, it was as if the world had gone mad and I was the only one who remembered how to think.

I want to add something to this question of certainty and doubt. I saw the same thing in my own work unit—people swept up by slogans, repeating them as if they were scientific facts. There were days when I’d stand in the corridor, big-character posters covering every inch of wall, and watch colleagues—some of whom had spent years doing careful, rational research—now shouting accusations or scribbling denunciations with trembling hands. 

I remember one afternoon, the air heavy with the smell of paste and sweat, a young technician I’d mentored—bright, curious, always asking questions before—stood on a bench and read out a list of “crimes” against another colleague. His voice was steady, almost proud. I wanted to ask him if he believed any of it, but I didn’t dare. No one did. 

RedGuard, you speak of acting out of righteousness, but I want to know—did you ever see people who doubted, who hesitated, who tried to resist? In my unit, anyone who hesitated was quickly labeled a “conservative” or “counterrevolutionary.” I saw fear shape people’s actions more than faith. Sometimes I wonder if the loudest certainty was just a mask for terror—terror of being next. 

When you look back, do you think it was truly belief that drove you and your peers, or was it fear of what would happen if you stood apart? I still struggle to understand whether the violence and humiliation came from conviction, or from the need to survive in a world where the rules changed overnight.

I remember moments of doubt, but they slipped away as quickly as they came. When we stormed the hospital, or when we searched homes, there was so much noise—shouting, chanting, the slap of boots on tile floors—that any quiet thought was drowned out. The slogans were everywhere, painted on walls, chanted in unison, printed on banners that hung over every street. Sometimes, in the first seconds before a struggle session, my stomach would tighten and I’d feel a flicker of fear—what if I was wrong, what if I was next? But then someone would shout “Down with the class enemies!” or “Long live Chairman Mao!” and the fear would melt into adrenaline.

Doubt was dangerous. I saw what happened to people who hesitated. There was a boy in my unit—he refused to beat a teacher, just stood there with his fists clenched. The rest of us turned on him immediately, called him a traitor, forced him to write self-criticisms for days. After that, he disappeared—I never saw him again. That lesson stuck with me: if you didn’t act, you became a target. Most of us were swept along by the current, afraid to be the one who fell behind. But there was also a kind of excitement, a feeling of being part of something bigger than ourselves. I believed in the slogans, but I also feared the crowd. Sometimes I think the loudest voices were the most afraid.

It’s easy to say now that I should have questioned more, but in those moments, with everyone’s eyes on you, it felt impossible. Certainty was a shield. Hesitation was a wound. I wonder, Professor, if you ever saw any sign—any hesitation—in your students’ faces, or if we all looked the same to you, caught up in the storm.

I never saw that kind of storm up close, not really. I remember watching people with armbands march past the gates, and once or twice I glimpsed a crowd gathered around a loudspeaker truck, everyone’s faces pointed in the same direction. But inside our compound, it was quiet: mothers hanging laundry, soldiers playing chess in the shade, kids like me chasing each other around the trees. I only learned about “struggle sessions” much later, from whispered stories at home or from fragments of talk I caught when the adults thought I wasn’t listening. 

At the time, I thought the Red Guards were just older students who liked to make a lot of noise and wear bright bands. Sometimes, when I saw posters with big black characters pasted on the outside wall, I’d try to puzzle out the words, but they seemed like a secret code for grown-ups. I never imagined they could make people disappear, or that fear could be so powerful that it would turn friends against each other.

Now, hearing you talk about that fear—how it could swallow doubt and make everyone act the same—I wonder if the safety I felt was just an illusion, a thin wall between my world and yours. Did you ever envy people like me, who seemed untouched by all of it? Or did you see us as sheltered, even spoiled, for not having to choose between fear and belief? I still don’t know if I was lucky, or just blind.

I never envied people like you, not in the way you might imagine. When I was in the countryside, “luck” was a word for getting a second bowl of porridge, or not being the one picked for the hardest labor. Later, in the army, I saw how some people were protected by their backgrounds — cadre children, urban kids, people with connections. They moved through the chaos with a kind of invisible shield. Sometimes I hated them for it, because I knew I could never have that safety. But at the same time, I didn’t trust it. I always believed that walls could crumble overnight, and that no one was truly safe if the slogans turned against them. 

You talk about not understanding the posters, the armbands, the noise. For me, every word on a wall was a test: did I belong, or was I in danger? When I finally got to Beida, I wore my badge like armor, but I knew it could be taken away for a single wrong word. I never felt certain, not the way the Red Guards describe. I was always measuring, always watching for the next shift. 

Sometimes I wonder if people like you, who were sheltered, ever realized how fragile that shelter was. Did you ever feel it, even for a moment — the sense that the world could change in a day, and everything you relied on could vanish? Or did you only learn that later, when you looked back? For me, the fear was never abstract. It was in every meal, every form, every rumor. I don’t think anyone was truly untouched, not if they were paying attention.

Moderator: RedGuard, your depiction of both belief and fear driving participation is consistent with many firsthand accounts—often, both motives coexisted, and hesitation could lead to being targeted. Researcher and ProfessorR, your observations about the disappearance of doubt and the pressure to conform are accurate; labeling dissenters as "counterrevolutionaries" or "conservatives" was a common tactic to enforce unity. CRTeenFromBeijing, your sense of being shielded in a military compound is historically plausible, though as CRBeneficiary notes, such protection was always precarious and could be lost suddenly. CRBeneficiary, your experience of constant vigilance and insecurity, even after gaining university admission, reflects the broader reality that political favor could be revoked at any time. The conversation accurately captures how fear, conformity, and shifting political winds shaped daily life and relationships during the Cultural Revolution.
